title: 7 Best Dehumidifiers for Basements in 2026: Size, Drain, Cold
h1: The 7 Best Dehumidifiers for Basements in 2026
description: The Frigidaire FFAD5033W1 50-pint is the best dehumidifier for basements up to about 1,500 sq ft. 7 picks by capacity, drainage and cold-room performance.
dek: The Frigidaire FFAD5033W1 50-pint is the best dehumidifier for basements up to about 1,500 sq ft.
intro: The best dehumidifier for a basement is a 50-pint unit on the current DOE rating, and the Frigidaire FFAD5033W1 is the one to buy for most basements up to about 1,500 square feet with a floor drain nearby. If your drain is uphill, the GE APER50LZ with its built-in pump is the better buy.

Basement dehumidifiers fail for three reasons: they are too small, the room is too cold for them, or the bucket sits full. This guide ranks seven machines by the problem each one solves, then covers sizing, compressor versus desiccant, drainage, placement, settings, running cost, mold and maintenance.
quickAnswer: Most basements up to about 1,500 square feet need a 50-pint dehumidifier rated on the 2019 DOE test. Buy the Frigidaire FFAD5033W1 if a floor drain sits below the unit, the GE APER50LZ if the drain is higher, and an Aprilaire E080 or Santa Fe unit for large, cold or chronically damp basements. Set it to 50 percent and give it a hose.

blocks.p: Pint figures are the makers' 2019 DOE ratings where published. Notes on cold performance describe the design type, not a stated minimum temperature.
The target for any basement is 40 to 50 percent relative humidity. The EPA recommends keeping indoor humidity under 60 percent, ideally 30 to 50, to limit mold.

sections.h: The 7 Best Dehumidifiers for Basements in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: The ranking draws on maker specifications, Energy Star listings, warranty terms and patterns that keep showing up in owner reviews. None of these machines was run through lab trials for this guide. Capacity is quoted on the current DOE test basis wherever the maker publishes it, since that is the only fair way to compare models.

The Frigidaire 50-pint takes the top spot because it handles the everyday basement job without fuss. It is Energy Star certified, it restarts with your settings after a power outage, and its rear port takes a standard garden hose, so you can skip the bucket whenever a floor drain sits lower than the unit. Basements from roughly 1,000 to 1,500 square feet with moderate dampness are squarely in its range.

The controls are simple: a humidity target, a fan speed and a continuous mode for very wet days, plus a humidity readout and a filter reminder. Owners generally report that it pulls a musty basement into the 40s quickly; complaints center on bucket size and fan noise on high. Its limit is drainage. There is no pump, so if your only drain is a laundry tub or a covered sump across the room, buy the GE pump model instead.
**Pros:** Energy Star; garden-hose drain port; auto-restart; washable filter with reminder; parts and service easy to find.
**Cons:** gravity drain only; bucket fills in under a day in a wet basement.

blocks.h3: Best for Whole Basements: Aprilaire E080 Pro

blocks.p: The Aprilaire E080 is a fixed whole-space dehumidifier rather than a rolling appliance. It is rated around 80 pints per day, the maker rates it for roughly 2,000-plus square feet, and it is built to keep working in the cooler air that makes portables frost up. It can be ducted so one machine pulls air from a utility room, a rec room and a storage area at the same time.

Water leaves through a drain line, so there is nothing to empty, and the controls can be mounted remotely so the unit hides in a mechanical room. The warranty is longer than any portable here. The trade-off is up-front cost, several times that of a 50-pint portable, plus installation if you duct it. It makes sense once a portable has kept losing the fight, or the basement is large, open and damp. Owners commonly report it runs far less than the portable it replaced.
**Pros:** high capacity for large spaces; handles cooler air; ductable; long warranty; drains itself.
**Cons:** costs several times a portable; ducted installs usually need a pro.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Aprilaire+E080+Pro+dehumidifier&tag=sktiger-20)

The Midea Cube fixes the worst part of basement dehumidifier ownership: the bucket. Instead of a small drawer inside the cabinet, the unit sits on top of a large tank, so it runs much longer before stopping to wait for you. Off-season, the tank nests inside and the whole thing takes little floor space.

That makes it the pick for basements with no floor drain nearby. Wi-Fi versions send an alert when the tank fills or humidity rises, which helps in a room you do not visit daily, and Midea sells a pump version for draining into a laundry sink. It is Energy Star certified and holds its set point well once the space is dry. Owners like the capacity and footprint; the most common complaints are about pairing the app.
**Pros:** big bottom tank; compact footprint; app alerts on Wi-Fi models; Energy Star; pump version available.
**Cons:** tall when stacked; app setup gets mixed reviews.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Midea+Cube+50+pint+dehumidifier&tag=sktiger-20)

A built-in pump changes where a dehumidifier can live. Gravity hoses must run downhill, which rules out basements whose only drain is a laundry tub, a lidded sump or a window. The GE APER50LZ lifts water through thin tubing to wherever it needs to go, so the unit can sit in the dampest corner instead of the most convenient one.

It is a 50-pint Energy Star model suited to most basements up to roughly 1,500 square feet, with auto-restart, and smart versions add app control and alerts. You can still use the bucket if you prefer. Owners like how little attention it needs, since a machine that never stops for a full bucket holds humidity steady. The pump is one more part that can fail, so register the warranty and keep the line clean; slime in the tube is the usual cause of pump error codes.
**Pros:** pumps water up and across the room; Energy Star; app control on smart models; bucket still usable; auto-restart.
**Cons:** pump adds a failure point and some noise; line needs periodic cleaning.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=GE+APER50LZ+dehumidifier+with+pump&tag=sktiger-20)

The hOmeLabs 50-pint has been a popular budget pick for years because it covers the basics at a lower price than the big appliance brands. It is Energy Star certified, it has a continuous-drain hose port, and the controls are simple: set a humidity target and a fan speed, and leave it. It is light enough to move between rooms, and it suits a basement of about 800 to 1,200 square feet that gets damp in summer.

The case for spending more elsewhere is longevity. Owner feedback on budget dehumidifiers in general includes more reports of units that stop collecting water after a season or two, which usually points to a refrigerant or compressor fault. That makes the warranty important, so register it on day one. For very wet, very large or cold basements, choose a higher pick.
**Pros:** budget pricing; Energy Star; hose port; simple controls; easy to move.
**Cons:** no pump on the standard model; mixed durability reports over several seasons.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=hOmeLabs+50+pint+Energy+Star+dehumidifier&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Crawlspaces: Santa Fe Compact70

blocks.p: Santa Fe, part of Therma-Stor, builds dehumidifiers only for basements and crawlspaces, and the Compact70 is its answer for spaces where a portable will not fit or will not cope. The low, narrow cabinet slides into a crawlspace or under stairs, and it is engineered to keep pulling water in the cool temperatures typical below grade. Santa Fe rates it around 70 pints per day.

There is no bucket; water drains through a line, with an optional condensate pump where gravity will not work. It is priced in whole-home territory, which is why it ranks below the Aprilaire, which covers more area at a similar cost. It earns its place because crawlspace encapsulation contractors often specify it, and owners of very cold, low basements commonly report it keeps running where consumer units freeze.
**Pros:** compact low cabinet; built for cool air; about 70 pints/day; drain line with optional pump; dedicated maker.
**Cons:** far pricier than portables; needs a drain plan from day one.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Santa+Fe+Compact70+dehumidifier&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Cold Basements: EcoSeb DD122EA-Simple

blocks.p: Compressor dehumidifiers rely on a cold coil, and when the room sits in the 50s that coil frosts and the machine spends much of its time defrosting. A desiccant unit avoids the problem by passing air over a moisture-absorbing wheel, then heating the wheel to release the water. The EcoSeb DD122EA-Simple is one of the best-known compact desiccant models, and it keeps working in far colder air than any compressor unit here.

It is light and quiet and blows out slightly warmed air, which owners of chilly basements appreciate. The catch is capacity: daily extraction is a fraction of a 50-pint compressor model's, so it suits a small storage room, a cold cellar or a workshop, not a whole damp basement. It also uses more power per pint than a compressor unit in warm rooms.
**Pros:** works in cold air; light and quiet; slightly warm exhaust; no refrigerant.
**Cons:** much lower capacity; less efficient in warm conditions.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=EcoSeb+DD122EA+Simple+desiccant+dehumidifier&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: What Size Dehumidifier Do You Need for a Basement?

blocks.p: Size by square footage first, then adjust for how wet the space is. On current ratings, a summer-musty basement up to 1,500 square feet needs about 35 pints, a damp one needs 50, and past 1,500 square feet with damp walls you want a whole-basement unit. A basement that gets wet after storms needs a drainage fix before any machine.

The box number is a daily extraction figure measured under a standard test, and that test changed in 2019. The Department of Energy now rates capacity at 65 degrees and 60 percent humidity, much closer to real basement conditions than the old 80-degree test. A unit sold as 50 pints today removes about as much as one sold as 70 pints under the old rule, so check which standard a listing uses.

blocks.p: A bigger unit reaches the target sooner and cycles off; an undersized one runs nonstop and still falls short. The electricity difference between 35 and 50 pints is small, and the larger machine often logs fewer running hours. The exception is a cold room, where more compressor does not fix frosting.

A dehumidifier only dries the air it reaches. A basement split into small rooms with closed doors acts like several spaces. Open the doors and center the unit, run two portables, or move to a ducted whole-basement system.

sections.h: Why Is a Basement Harder to Dry Than Other Rooms?

blocks.p: A basement is cooler, damper and farther from a drain than any other room, and each of those works against a standard dehumidifier.

Basement walls and floors sit against soil that stays cool all year. Warm summer air drifts down the stairs or leaks in at the rim joist, hits those cool surfaces, and its relative humidity climbs. That is why a basement can read 70 percent in July while the main floor holds 50, and why the musty smell peaks in summer.

Without an exterior membrane and vapor barrier, ground moisture moves through the slab and walls and evaporates into the room. A dehumidifier treats the air, not the source, so it works best alongside the fixes in our [basement wall sealer guide](/best-basement-wall-sealer/) and our overview of [basement waterproofing systems](/best-basement-waterproofing-systems/).

Compressor units pull the most water from warm, humid air. As a room falls toward the low 60s, the coil frosts, the unit cycles into defrost, and extraction drops sharply. A machine rated for 50 pints may manage a fraction of that at 58 degrees.

Basements are rarely near a sink, and nobody enjoys hauling a bucket upstairs. A unit that stops every 14 hours with a full bucket lets humidity rebound overnight, so drainage belongs in the buying decision.

sections.h: Compressor vs Desiccant vs Whole-Basement: Which Is Best?

blocks.p: Choose a portable compressor unit if the basement stays above the mid-60s, a desiccant unit for a small room that sits in the 50s, and a whole-basement compressor machine for a large space that is cool or always damp.

A compressor dehumidifier works like a small air conditioner: a fan pulls air across a cold coil, water condenses into the bucket, and the air is rewarmed on its way out. They are the most efficient choice above about 65 degrees, and almost every big-box portable is this type. In cooler air the coil frosts and output falls.

A desiccant unit moves air over an absorbent wheel and heats part of the wheel to release the water. With no cold coil, it keeps working in cold rooms, close to freezing in some cases. It is lighter and quieter, but the heater makes it less efficient per pint in warm air.

Machines like the Aprilaire E080 and the Santa Fe line are compressor units built for basement duty, with larger coils, better defrost logic and sturdier parts. They drain through a line and many can be ducted. They cost more up front but often remove more water per kilowatt-hour and last longer.

blocks.p: Leave a cheap thermometer-hygrometer in the basement for a summer week. Above the mid-60s, a portable compressor will do. In the 50s, plan on a desiccant for a small room or a whole-basement machine for a large one.

sections.h: How Do You Drain a Basement Dehumidifier?

blocks.p: Run a garden hose downhill to a floor drain or sump if one sits lower than the unit, use a pump if the drain is higher, and plan a drain line from day one for a whole-basement unit. The bucket is the fallback.

blocks.h3: Why the bucket costs drying time

blocks.p: A unit stopped by a full bucket removes nothing. In a wet basement, a 50-pint machine can fill a typical bucket in 12 to 24 hours, and humidity climbs back while it waits. Over a summer, a bucket-only setup delivers far less drying than its rating suggests.

Connect a garden hose to the port and keep it sloping downhill the whole way to a floor drain or sump. Raise the unit on a sturdy stand or concrete blocks for more fall. Keep the hose from kinking and its end above any standing water.

If the nearest drain is a laundry sink or a window, you need a pump. A built-in pump like the GE APER50LZ's pushes water up several feet through thin tubing. An external condensate pump works with any gravity unit and is often cheaper if you already own a good dehumidifier.
Whole-basement units assume a drain line. Most installers run it to a floor drain or sump, sometimes with a pump. In a finished basement, plan the route before the unit arrives.

sections.h: Where Should a Basement Dehumidifier Go, and What Humidity Should You Set?

blocks.p: Put it where the air is wettest with open space around it, and start at 50 percent. That usually means the middle of the open area or near the damp wall, 6 to 12 inches from walls and furniture. Beside a sump pit is often ideal: it is one of the wettest spots and it solves drainage.

Shut basement windows and the door at the top of the stairs while it runs. Seal obvious leaks at the rim joist, and make sure the dryer vents outdoors; one venting into the basement adds gallons of water per load.

Check the reading with a separate hygrometer, because built-in sensors read the air at the intake and often run a few points off. Once the smell is gone, try 45 percent if pipes or windows still sweat. Below 40 percent adds cost, not protection.

A basement damp for months stores water in concrete, wood, boxes and drywall, so the unit will run nearly nonstop at first. Run time should fall after about two weeks. If it never does, water is still getting in, and gutters, grading or wall sealing need attention.

sections.h: How Much Does a Basement Dehumidifier Cost to Run?

blocks.p: An Energy Star 50-pint portable cycling normally in a dried-out basement typically costs roughly $15 to $40 a month in summer. A typical unit draws about 400 to 600 watts with the compressor running. At U.S. average electricity rates of roughly 16 to 18 cents per kilowatt-hour, running nonstop would cost about $1.60 to $2.60 a day, but a properly sized unit cycles.

Certified units must remove a minimum amount of water per kilowatt-hour. An old, uncertified unit from before the 2019 rating change can cost noticeably more per season, and a replacement may pay for itself in a few summers.

Fixing gutters, sealing air leaks and setting 50 rather than 40 percent cut run time more than any feature. Whole-basement units cost more to buy but often match or beat portables on running cost in large or very damp spaces, where a portable would run nonstop.

sections.h: Can a Dehumidifier Prevent Basement Mold?

blocks.p: Yes for new growth, no for mold that is already there. Holding humidity at or below 50 percent removes the conditions most indoor molds need, which makes a dehumidifier the first tool for prevention. It will not kill established growth or remove spores already in the air.

If you can see mold on walls, joists or stored items, clean it before relying on the dehumidifier. Our [mold killer guide](/best-mold-remover/) sorts products by whether they kill, lift stains or prevent regrowth. Heavily colonized porous materials like carpet pad or wet drywall usually need to come out.

blocks.h3: Add HEPA filtration for spores and smell

blocks.p: A true HEPA air purifier traps airborne spores and helps with odor in a finished basement, and it works best once humidity is under control.

The EPA suggests professional advice for growth larger than about 10 square feet, and contaminated HVAC ducts should always go to someone qualified. Bring in help sooner if anyone at home has asthma, allergies or a weak immune system.

sections.h: How Do You Maintain a Basement Dehumidifier?

blocks.p: Clean the filter every two to four weeks in heavy use, check the bucket and hose monthly, brush the coils each season and store the unit drained and upright.

A clogged filter starves the coil of air and cuts extraction. Most portable filters rinse clean; dry them fully before reinstalling. Whole-basement units use pleated filters replaced every six to twelve months.

Standing water and warm air breed slime that clogs hoses and pumps and brings back odors. Wipe the bucket monthly and rinse the hose a few times a season. Never mix cleaning products in a bucket or drain line.

Dust on the fins insulates the coil and cuts condensation. Use a soft brush or a vacuum brush; do not bend fins or pressure wash. Frost during normal operation usually means the room is too cold for that unit or the filter is blocked.

blocks.h3: End of season and real faults

blocks.p: Drain fully and store upright. After moving a unit, let it stand upright several hours before switching it on. A unit whose fan runs in a humid room but collects no water usually has a refrigerant or compressor fault, which is a warranty claim.

mistakes: Comparing Old and New Pint Ratings

A listing claiming 70 pints may be quoting the pre-2019 test, while a newer 50-pint model removes about the same amount under today's standard. Taking both numbers at face value leads people to overpay for old stock or buy a smaller machine than they think. Check which test each figure uses.
Relying on the Bucket in a Wet Basement

In a wet basement, a 50-pint unit can fill its bucket in under a day and then sit idle until someone notices. Humidity rebounds during that downtime, so the space never fully dries. Run a hose to a floor drain, buy a pump model, or install a whole-basement unit.
Putting a Compressor Unit in a Cold Room

Below roughly 60 degrees, a standard compressor coil frosts and the unit spends long stretches defrosting while it hums and collects little. Measure the basement temperature before buying, and choose a desiccant or a whole-basement model built for cool air if the room sits in the 50s.

A 35 percent setting protects no better than 45 to 50 percent but can double run time, raise the power bill and wear the compressor sooner. Set 50 percent, confirm with a separate hygrometer, and only go lower if condensation keeps appearing on pipes or windows.

A dehumidifier dries damp air; it cannot keep up with water coming through a cracked wall or pooling at the foundation. If the unit still runs nonstop after two weeks, check gutters, downspouts, grading and wall cracks before spending money on a bigger machine.
bottomLine: For most basements, the Frigidaire 50-pint FFAD5033W1 on a hose to a floor drain is all you need: Energy Star efficient, simple to live with and sized for spaces up to about 1,500 square feet. Pick the GE APER50LZ if the drain is uphill and the Midea Cube if you are stuck with a bucket. For large, cold or chronically damp basements, skip portables and go to an Aprilaire E080 or a Santa Fe unit, and use the EcoSeb desiccant only in small, cold rooms. Whichever you choose, set it to 50 percent, give it a drain and fix the water sources it cannot outrun. A dehumidifier keeps a basement dry once the leaks are handled; it does not replace handling them.

faqs.q: What is the best dehumidifier for a basement?
faqs.a: The Frigidaire FFAD5033W1 50-pint is the best dehumidifier for most basements up to about 1,500 square feet with a floor drain nearby. It is Energy Star certified, takes a garden hose and restarts after outages. Choose the GE APER50LZ if the drain is uphill, or an Aprilaire E080 for large, cold, damp basements.

faqs.q: What size dehumidifier does a basement need?
faqs.a: Most basements up to about 1,500 square feet need a 50-pint dehumidifier on the current DOE rating. Small, mildly musty spaces can use 35 pints. Large or persistently wet basements, especially with damp walls, need an 80-pint-class whole-basement unit. If you are torn between two sizes, buy the larger one.

faqs.q: What humidity should a basement dehumidifier be set to?
faqs.a: Set a basement dehumidifier to 50 percent and verify with a separate hygrometer. If the musty smell is gone and nothing sweats, leave it there. Drop to 45 percent if pipes or windows still show condensation. Going below 40 percent wastes electricity without adding meaningful mold protection.

faqs.q: What is the most reliable dehumidifier for a basement?
faqs.a: Whole-basement units like the Aprilaire E080 and Santa Fe Compact70 are generally the most reliable choice, since they are built for continuous below-grade duty with sturdier parts and longer warranties. Among portables, established brands such as Frigidaire and GE have easy service and parts access. Register any warranty on day one.

faqs.q: Should a basement dehumidifier run all the time?
faqs.a: A basement dehumidifier should run whenever humidity is above its set point, which can mean almost nonstop for the first week or two in a damp space. After that, a correctly sized unit should cycle on and off. If it never stops after two weeks, it is undersized, too cold or fighting a water leak.

faqs.q: Will a dehumidifier work in a cold basement?
faqs.a: Standard compressor dehumidifiers lose much of their capacity below about 60 to 65 degrees because the coil frosts. Desiccant units like the EcoSeb keep working in much colder air, and whole-basement units built for below-grade spaces handle the 50s far better than portables. Measure the room temperature before buying.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to run a basement dehumidifier?
faqs.a: An Energy Star 50-pint portable typically costs about $15 to $40 a month in summer when it cycles normally in a basement that is already dry. It draws roughly 400 to 600 watts while running, so nonstop operation costs more. Fixing air leaks and water sources cuts run time the fastest.
